label: BOUNDARIES WITHOUT A QUARREL · TWO DAYS BEFORE THE MOVE
deadline: Answer to Anya — on Saturday morning

ui.hubLead: Choose how to spend this slot. You can’t do everything.
ui.hubTip: There are more meetings than slots: each one closes off another, and what you skip leaves a mark too.

intro.title: Boundaries without a quarrel
paragraphs: Your friend Anya is moving on Saturday and asks you to help all day. You have a deadline on Monday, and your energy is running out.
How do you say “I can do this, but not everything” without losing someone close? There’s no right ending; every answer has its price.
intro.disclaimer: A fictional story. Choices in the game send nothing to anyone and don’t judge your real relationships.

clues.own_deadline: The report is due on Monday: about six hours of solid work.
clues.anya_needs: Anya: thirty boxes, a wardrobe and a bike. The heaviest part is the wardrobe and loading.
clues.real_need: Anya: “The wardrobe and loading are the heaviest.” The rest can be done without you.
clues.helpers: Dima and two more friends are already coming; the van is rented until two in the afternoon.

scenes.title: A message from Anya
scenes.intro: Wednesday evening. You’ve barely sat down after work when a voice message from Anya arrives: she’s moving on Saturday and really asks for help — “at least for the day”. And on Monday your report is due, which you haven’t started.

line.text: I wouldn’t ask anyone, but I have deadlines: I hand over the keys on Sunday. You’ll come, right?

objects.label: Your own plans
objects.text: In your notes: Saturday — “finish the report”. Next to it: “rest before I snap”.

objects.label: Voice message
objects.text: Anya sounds tired, she talks fast and jokes between sentences. It’s clear asking isn’t easy for her.

choices.text: “Of course, I’ll come for the whole day.”
choices.result: Anya exhales: “Thank you, you’re the best.” It feels good — and immediately heavy: Saturday is now fully taken.

choices.text: “I need to think, I’ll answer tomorrow.”
choices.result: Anya answers faster than you expect: “OK. Just don’t disappear, alright?”

choices.text: “I want to help, but I have a deadline on Monday. Let’s work out what exactly is needed.”
choices.result: A pause. “Oh, I didn’t know about the deadline. Let’s work it out — what matters more is not being left alone.”
choices.trace: Named the limit and the wish to help.

choices.text: Read it and don’t answer.
choices.result: The message is marked as read. Silence buys you the evening — and drags awkwardness along with it.

scenes.title: Your own tasks
scenes.teaser: See what’s really needed for Monday.
scenes.intro: You open the report and calculate how many hours it really needs and when you have them.

objects.label: Calculation
objects.text: About six hours of solid work. If you skip Saturday, they fit into Sunday, but with no margin.

objects.label: Calendar
objects.text: Saturday is an empty box, Sunday too. Nothing is protected yet.

choices.text: Block three hours on Sunday in the calendar for the report.
choices.result: The box in the calendar is coloured in. Now it’s not “if there’s time left” but an agreement with yourself.

choices.text: Start the report right now, with a tired head.
choices.result: An hour later you have two paragraphs and red eyes. But the fear of “not even started” is gone.

choices.text: Close the laptop: not now.
choices.result: The relief is short. The deadline hasn’t gone anywhere — it will just wait for you on Monday.

scenes.title: Calling Anya

cases.text: Anya called twice.
Find out what’s really needed.

scenes.intro: Anya picks up right away. Boxes rustle in the background, tape snaps.

cases.text: I’m so glad you’re coming for the whole day! I made a plan for you…
You disappeared. I thought you were offended. What happened?
I really don’t want to pressure you. I’m just afraid I won’t manage without people.

objects.label: Boxes
objects.text: Anya counts aloud: thirty boxes, a wardrobe, a bike. Most of it is already packed.

objects.label: List
objects.text: Anya’s list: assembling the wardrobe and transport. The rest — “if we have time”.

choices.text: Ask: “What’s definitely needed, and what can be done without me?”
choices.result: Anya thinks. “The wardrobe and loading are the heaviest. The rest I’ll manage myself, or Dima will help.”
choices.trace: It became clearer what exactly is needed.

choices.text: Just listen to her: she hasn’t talked about all this out loud for a long time.
choices.result: She talks about the break-up, the rented flat, the fear of being alone. You barely speak, and she’s clearly feeling lighter.

choices.text: Promise to come in the morning, the rest “depending on how it goes”.
choices.result: Anya calms down. But “depending on how it goes” tells neither of you when you’ll leave.

scenes.title: Dima with the car
scenes.intro: You meet Dima at the metro — he’s carrying parts for the wardrobe and mentions in passing how they arranged things with Anya.

line.text: We have a van for the morning and two more friends. Anya isn’t the type to ask for too much, she’s just shy about asking.

objects.label: Van
objects.text: The van is rented until two in the afternoon. There are already three movers, not counting you.

choices.text: Ask: “If I only come for the loading, will that help?”
choices.result: “Loading is the most important part. After two we’ll manage on our own,” Dima answers. Sounds like a real plan.
choices.trace: It turned out a few hours would be enough.

choices.text: Just chat without asking anything.
choices.result: Dima talks about the neighbours and laughs at his own jokes. You part as friends, but nothing is clearer.

choices.text: Offer to go with them for the whole day — “just in case”.
choices.result: Dima nods: “Great, so you’re with us until evening.” The offer flew out faster than you could think.
choices.trace: Offered the whole day without thinking it through.

scenes.title: Coffee with Anya
scenes.teaser: Anya invites you for coffee before the move.
scenes.intro: Anya arrives with red eyes and a bag of papers. It’s clear holding it together isn’t easy for her.

line.text: I don’t want to look pathetic. It’s just that everything piled up at once.

objects.label: Papers
objects.text: The lease, the handover form, a list of things. Signatures in three places.

objects.label: Coffee
objects.text: Anya ordered your favourite before even asking. Care is in the little things.

choices.text: Say: “I’ll come for a few hours and help with the loading.”
choices.result: Anya nods and writes it in her notebook. “Loading is a lot.” It’s clear she expected less and is grateful anyway.
choices.trace: Offered a specific part of the help.

choices.text: Say: “I can’t do the whole day, but on Sunday evening I’ll come with food and help you set up.”
choices.result: Anya blinks: “I actually need that more — the first evening there will be empty.” The boundary doesn’t push her away; it moves the help somewhere else.
choices.trace: Offered help in a different way.

choices.text: Start apologising: “Sorry I can’t do more.”
choices.result: Anya waves it away: “Don’t be silly, don’t apologise.” But for the whole coffee you talk about your guilt, not her move.

scenes.title: Guilt
scenes.intro: You notice that all day you’ve been thinking not about the report or the move, but about “am I a good friend”.

objects.label: Note
objects.text: You write: “What do I owe? What do I want? What am I able to do?” Three columns, still empty.

choices.text: Fill in the three columns honestly.
choices.result: It comes out: owe — to be there, want — to help in my own way, able — a few hours. A steady formula you can lean on.

choices.text: Drown it out with a TV series.
choices.result: Two hours of lightness. Then the guilt returns, but quieter.

scenes.title: Answering Anya
scenes.teaser: Write a message so that it’s heard.
scenes.intro: Late in the evening you open your chat with Anya and write a draft.

objects.label: Draft
objects.text: Three versions: warm and clear, vague, and “we’ll decide later”. You need one.

choices.text: Write: “I’ll help with the loading in the morning and come on Sunday evening. I can’t do the whole day — I have a report.”
choices.result: The message goes. A minute later: “Thanks for being honest.” Your hands stop shaking.

choices.text: Write: “I’ll try, we’ll see.”
choices.result: The message breaks nothing — and solves nothing. At night you catch yourself checking your phone.

choices.text: Write a long apology with five excuses.
choices.result: It comes out three screens long. Anya answers “ok” — and you only feel worse.

scenes.title: A walk
scenes.intro: You go out without a goal. The wind is cold, the air is clean.

objects.label: Bench
objects.text: The bench is empty. You can sit down and decide nothing.

choices.text: Walk to the embankment.
choices.result: Over the water your head clears. “No” stops sounding like betrayal.

choices.text: Come back after one block.
choices.result: A short pause. Good to have somewhere to come back to.

final.title: Decision
final.subtitle: the movers arrive at nine
final.ask: What do you say to Anya?
intro: Saturday, 8:40. The courtyard, the van, boxes by the entrance.

cases.text: You remember you promised the whole day. The report waits at home as a reminder.
You mentioned Sunday — but now it needs to be said out loud.
Anya doesn’t know yet what you’ll decide, and it shows on her face.

intro.text: Dima nods to you from the cab — good that you talked in advance.

lines.text: Can you really do the whole day? I don’t want you to be angry later.
Thanks for telling me in advance. Let’s see what works best.
You came. That already means a lot to me.

options.text: Stay for the whole day, as promised.

cases.text: You pick up the first box. Your hands get used to it quickly, your head more slowly: it’s already counting the report hours.
You stay. It’s your own decision, but you catch yourself doing it out of “I have to”, not “I want to”.

options.text: Help with the loading in the morning and leave after lunch.

lock.reason: It’s still unclear what exactly you can do. A talk with Anya or Dima and a calculation of your own time would help.

options.result: You name the time: “From nine to one.” Anya nods and immediately plans what to give you. Defined hours work better than a promise of “the whole day”.

options.text: Don’t go on Saturday, but come on Sunday evening with food.

lock.reason: For a refusal to sound like care rather than escape, you need a plan of your own: at least your own time for the report or an honest talk with Anya.

options.result: You say it straight: “I can’t do Saturday, I have a report. I’ll come on Sunday evening with food.” Anya is silent for a second and hugs you: “OK. I’m actually looking forward to that more.”

options.text: Ask for another day: you’ll answer in the evening.

lock.reason: Asking for a delay should have happened earlier — on the morning of the move it already lets people down.

options.result: Anya says: “If it’s before lunch — OK. But I need to know.” You get time, but it’s already limited.

cases.text: The whole day — but not out of “I have to”
A few hours that are honest
No, but with a different “yes”
Time that ran out anyway
You spent the whole day on your feet, carried boxes until dark, and the report still lies untouched. Anya is grateful, though she sees you’re tired.
You helped in the morning and left after lunch. The report on Sunday went calmly: three hours already protected in the calendar.
You didn’t go on Saturday and wrote honestly why. On Sunday you came with food and helped arrange the books: Anya laughed that the first dinner in a new flat is the best one.
You answered late. Anya managed with Dima’s help, but you can tell she was counting on you more.
Anya said: “You taught me to ask more specifically.” Boundaries and friendship turned out to fit in one room.
Things with Anya are still warm. She knows you don’t disappear, even when you can’t come.
Things with Anya are even. A slight aftertaste remains, but the conversation isn’t closed.
There’s still tension with Anya. Nobody has taken the first step towards talking yet.
You noticed: when you apologise a lot, a conversation about a boundary turns into a conversation about guilt.
A vague “depending on how it goes” reassured no one: neither you nor Anya.
You understand well where your boundary lies, and it shows in the little things.
Something became clearer: what you’re ready to share and in what form.
The boundary is still blurry. But the question “what can I actually do?” is already being asked.
